tracks.title: One release, every door
tracks.text: Lesson 07 point 7 — distribution. This one is a sub-lesson, under wbx. One release… every door. Here's the whole idea up front. Most tools fork into a dozen packaging pipelines that quietly disagree. This one has exactly one. A GitHub release, tagged wbx dash v… holding five native binaries and one wasm module. And every way to install the tool — curl… npm… self-upgrade… and the runtime image — is just a courier for the same bytes. [curious] Same bytes… different doors. Let's open the hood.

tracks.title: Three installs, three tools
tracks.text: First — three installs, three tools. Every ecosystem hands you an install ritual, and the rituals disagree. [sighs] The Homebrew formula is three versions behind, because a volunteer maintains it on weekends. The npm package wraps a binary in a download step that fails silently — and you find out at runtime, weeks later, when the command finally errors. The curl one-liner works, but feels like trusting a stranger with sudo. And six months on, you have three copies of the same tool fighting over your PATH… and no honest answer to the only question that matters. Which one does the shell actually find? Here's the deeper problem. Each lane is usually its own build — its own pipeline, its own packaging, its own version cadence. Three pipelines is three things that can drift apart. And they do.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Distribution is one GitHub release, tagged wbx dash v star, that every install lane — curl… npm… self-upgrade… and the runtime image — is a courier for. Same bytes, different doors. The word usually names a sprawl. Registries… mirrors… package formats… channels. Here it names a single artifact. A tag triggers one CI workflow. That workflow builds the binaries once, and attaches them to a release. And every door into the tool reads from that release. [excited] There is no second build. Nothing can drift… because there is only one thing to keep honest, and CI keeps it.

tracks.title: Anatomy of a release
tracks.text: Anatomy of a release. Let me walk you through what actually happens. Picture a single flow. At the top, a git tag — wbx dash v 0 point 13 point 0. That fires one workflow, which strips the prefix to get the version… and then it splits. On one branch, a native build matrix — five targets. On the other, a single wasm job. Both branches pour into one bright node in the middle — the release, holding five binaries plus wbx dot wasm. And from that one node, three arrows fan out — to curl… to npm… and to wbx upgrade. That fan-out is the entire mental model. One tag in… one release out… three lanes drinking from the same node. The five binaries are Apple Silicon and Intel Mac, x64 and arm64 Linux, and a Windows exe. The Intel Mac one is worth a note — it's cross-compiled on the Apple Silicon runner, because the Intel Mac runners are being retired and can queue forever. Now picture the release laid bare, a little tree of six files. First, wbx dash darwin dash arm64 — that's the curl lane on Apple Silicon, and the npm postinstall. Second, wbx dash darwin dash x64 — cross-compiled on the arm64 runner. Third and fourth, the two Linux binaries. Fifth, wbx dash windows dash x64 dot exe — npm lane only; curl tells Windows users to use WSL. And sixth… wbx dot wasm, for in-sandbox agents. One more touch — publishing is idempotent. The job tries to create the release, and if it already exists, it uploads and clobbers instead. Re-running never errors, never half-publishes.

tracks.title: The curl lane
tracks.text: The curl lane. curl, pipe to shell. The first door, and it's a plain POSIX script — about sixty lines, served as a static file. It does four things, in order, and each one is auditable. First… it discovers the latest tag — it asks the GitHub API for the releases, and greps the first tag name starting with wbx dash v. Second… it maps your machine to an asset name — uname gives the OS and the arch, which become darwin or linux, and arm64 or x64. Third… it downloads to a temp file, makes it executable, and moves it into place. And fourth… it runs wbx version as a smoke check — so a broken download fails right there, instead of next Tuesday. The install directory has a fallback — slash usr slash local slash bin if that's writable, otherwise dot local slash bin. And there are three knobs. First, WBX underscore VERSION — pin a specific release instead of latest. Second, WBX underscore INSTALL underscore DIR — choose where the binary lands. Third, WBX underscore REPO — point at a different repo's releases. [curious] One honest limit — it's macOS and Linux only. An unknown OS exits with… unsupported; Windows via WSL.

tracks.title: The npm lane
tracks.text: The npm lane. The npm package is a thin launcher — not a copy of the binary. It ships exactly three files — the launcher, the installer, and a readme — plus a postinstall hook that downloads the right native binary the moment you install it. And here's the clever part — how it finds the binary with no metadata service at all. CI stamps the package's version straight from the tag. So the package that calls itself 0 point 13 point 0 can compute its own download URL — releases slash download slash wbx dash v 0 point 13 point 0 slash wbx dash darwin dash arm64 — from nothing but its own version and your platform. [excited] The npm version and the release tag are lockstep, by construction. No version endpoint… no manifest… no call to resolve latest. Let me walk the install through, step by step. The install runs the postinstall. The postinstall computes the asset name from your platform and architecture. It requests that asset from the release… and GitHub answers not with bytes, but with a 302 redirect to its storage backend. So the installer follows redirects by hand — up to ten hops — and the bytes finally arrive. It writes them, sets the executable bit… and then runs one last safety check we'll come back to. The launcher itself is thirty-seven lines. It checks the binary exists, then separately that it's executable — two distinct messages, because the postinstall failed and the binary is not executable are different problems. If all is well, it spawns the native binary, inherits your terminal, and forwards the exit code. The Node process is a pass-through. The real wbx is the binary it launches.

tracks.title: The shadow check
tracks.text: The shadow check. Here's the scenario the npm lane is built to survive. You curl-installed wbx months ago, into slash usr slash local slash bin. And today, you npm-install it. Now there are two binaries on your PATH… and the one that wins is whichever directory comes first. The npm one you just installed might be invisible. So the installer walks every directory on your PATH, in order, looking for a file named wbx. If the first one it finds is a different file than the one it just installed… that earlier path is shadowing the new install. And it says so, by name. Picture the banner — a boxed warning that reads… wb PATH SHADOW WARNING… another wb binary was found earlier on your PATH, at slash usr slash local slash bin slash wbx. To fix, either remove the old binary, or adjust PATH so npm's bin directory comes first. The predicate is the whole insight. The first wbx on PATH that isn't the one we just wrote… is, by definition, the one that shadows it — because shells resolve left to right, and stop at the first hit. Walk in PATH order; compare resolved paths; that's exactly what the shell does at call time. And the table behind it tells a three-line story. The first directory holds the old curl binary — verdict, it shadows the new install. The next directory holds the one we just installed — but it's too late, never reached. And the third case — when the first hit IS ours — the check returns null… no shadow, and it prints nothing.

tracks.title: Failing loud, exiting zero
tracks.text: Failing loud, exiting zero. The npm lane has a design stance about failure, and it's the opposite of how most postinstalls behave. A postinstall download must never brick the install — if it exits non-zero, it takes the whole dependency install down with it. That's a terrible thing to do to someone who just wanted a CLI. But it also must never fail silently — because the silent postinstall is exactly the failure mode that makes people distrust npm-wrapped binaries. The resolution — on any download error, print a loud boxed banner… then exit zero. The banner is the signal. The zero keeps the install alive. And the banner is careful to tell you which of two situations you're in. One — the wb binary was NOT downloaded, running wb will fail. Or two — a previous binary is still present, and may work. [curious] Those are very different messages… and the installer knows which to say. It hands you both recovery commands right there — the curl lane as an escape hatch, and npm rebuild to retry. And the launcher is the backstop for anything that slips past. Run wbx with a missing or non-executable binary, and it prints its own fatal banner, with the same two fixes, and exits one. Loud at install time… loud at run time… never silent at either.

tracks.title: The binary replaces itself
tracks.text: The binary replaces itself. The third lane is wbx upgrade — the tool swapping itself for a newer copy. It locates its own executable on disk… and then does the most important thing first. It checks whether it lives inside a node modules directory. If any component of its path is node modules, it stops, and tells you to use npm instead. Picture the two outcomes side by side. Curl-installed, at slash usr slash local slash bin — it prints… upgraded, wbx 0 point 12 point 0 to 0 point 13 point 0. Npm-installed, path has node modules — it prints… installed via npm; upgrade with npm update dash g. That refusal is a feature, not a gap. File ownership inside node modules belongs to the package manager. A binary rewriting itself there would be fighting npm over which copy is real. So it declines… and points you at the command that respects npm's bookkeeping. For a curl-installed binary, it discovers the latest release the same way the shell script does, and compares it to its own compiled-in version. Same — it says already current, and stops. Different — it does an atomic swap, and let me walk that swap as a story. The running wbx asks the API for the latest tag, gets wbx dash v 0 point 13 point 0… and compares it to the version baked into itself at compile time. They differ, so it downloads the new bytes, and writes them to a sibling file — wbx dot new, right next to itself. It marks that new file executable. And then… the one move that makes this safe. It renames wbx dot new over wbx. [excited] Rename is atomic on the same filesystem — so there is never a moment where PATH holds a half-written binary. The running process keeps executing the old version it already loaded. The next invocation is the new one. And a crash mid-download leaves the old binary untouched. The curl lane's counterpart to all this is pinning — set WBX underscore VERSION to the version you want, in front of the curl command, and you install that exact release.

tracks.title: The fourth asset
tracks.text: The fourth asset. The sixth file in every release is wbx dot wasm, built for the wasm32 wasip1 target. It ships in the same release as the native binaries, because wbx is one crate compiled to two kinds of target — and that's the seam, a lesson of its own. This is the lane for the sandboxed future — a wasm module wbx that can run inside the engine's sandbox, alongside the workbooks it operates on. Two honest notes belong here. First — the wasm build of upgrade, and of open, deliberately bails, saying… upgrade needs the native binary. A module running inside a sandbox cannot rewrite its own file, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Second — the consumption side. The artifact ships, and it's the spec'd path for in-sandbox agents… but the runtime-side wiring that fetches that published wasm isn't visible in the code yet. It's the lane that exists for where this is going, stated plainly as that. Meanwhile, the runtime image doesn't download wbx from a release at all. Its Dockerfile compiles wbx from source in a build stage, and copies the stripped binary to slash usr slash local slash bin slash wbx. So the agents working inside the engine get a native wbx pinned to the image's exact commit — not downloaded, not wasm. Same source… a different door again. Built in place, at a known SHA.

tracks.title: What this doesn't solve
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what this doesn't solve. The one-artifact design buys a lot, but it has real edges, and naming them is the point. The npm lane's postinstall dies under npm install dash dash ignore dash scripts — no postinstall runs, no binary downloads. The spec actually describes a different shape — per-platform optional dependencies — that would survive that flag, because the platform binary arrives as a real dependency instead of a download step. The shipped implementation chose the single-package postinstall instead — one package to maintain, against five-plus registry packages. [curious] That's a deliberate trade, not an oversight. And if you do run ignore-scripts, the curl lane is your way in. The other edges, briefly. First — there's no Homebrew, apt, or winget. Second — the curl lane skips Windows entirely; that's npm, or WSL. Third — the atomic rename in upgrade is only atomic on the same filesystem, and needs write permission to the install directory. And fourth — the static binary claim is precise. wbx is built with rustls instead of OpenSSL, so there's no interpreter and no VM to install — but the Linux builds target gnu, not musl. So no runtime deps means no interpreter… not zero dynamic libraries. The table behind this lines the lanes up against what breaks them. curl breaks on Windows — escape to npm or WSL. npm breaks on ignore-scripts — escape to curl. upgrade breaks across filesystems — escape by reinstalling. And wasm — its consumption wiring is still landing; the native binary is the answer today.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is curl pipe shell safe here? It's about sixty lines of POSIX shell, served as a static file you can read before you run it — open it in a tab first. It discovers a tag, downloads an asset over HTTPS, moves it into place, and runs version. Auditable beats trusted. How do I pin a version? On curl, set WBX underscore VERSION before the script. On npm, ask for it directly — at sign work dot books slash cli, at 0 point 12 point 0 — and because version and tag are lockstep, that pins the binary too. I installed both curl and npm — which wins? Whichever directory comes first on PATH. Which is exactly what the shadow banner told you at install time. Why is the npm package at sign work dot books slash cli, not just wbx? The bare name was taken — the parent lesson covers it. How do agents inside the engine get wbx? They don't download it — the runtime image compiles it from source and bakes it in. And why two npm registries? npmjs, and a GitHub Packages mirror — the same launcher, two homes.

tracks.title: Back up to the command line
tracks.text: So that's distribution. One release, tagged wbx dash v… five binaries and a wasm module… and four couriers carrying the same bytes through four different doors. No second build. Nothing to drift. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson, and its parent is wbx — lesson seven — the command line itself, where the verbs the installed binary runs all live. And the neighbor worth a look is the seam — one crate, two targets — which is why a wasm asset exists at all. Everything here was just the couriers. Go meet the cargo.
